title: Tracking the Elusive Leopards of Yala: Block 1 vs Lunugamvehera
excerpt: Why our private naturalists frequently bypass congested Block 1 gate traffic to track resident apex predators along Lunugamvehera's quieter elephant corridors.

cover.alt: Sri Lankan leopard resting on a palu tree branch in Yala at dawn

content:
Yala has one of the highest densities of leopards anywhere in the world, and the Sri Lankan subspecies — *Panthera pardus kotiya* — is the island's top predator, with no lions or tigers to compete with. That is why travellers come from everywhere to see one. It is also why the main entrance can look like a car park at six in the morning.

Here is how I think about where to go.

## Block 1: famous for a reason

Block 1 is the most visited part of the park, and for good reason: the rocky outcrops, waterholes and open scrub make leopards relatively easy to see, especially in the dry months from February to June when animals gather around water.

### The downside

When a leopard is spotted, radios crackle and within minutes dozens of jeeps race to the same bend. Engines run, people shout, and the leopard usually leaves. It is not the experience I want for my guests — or for the animal.

### How we do Block 1 well

- **Enter at gate opening** and head away from the main convoy.
- **Choose a waterhole and wait,** engine off, instead of chasing radio calls.
- **Leave a sighting** if it becomes crowded. There will be another.
- **Stay through late morning,** when most jeeps return for breakfast and the park becomes quiet again.

## Block 5 and Lunugamvehera: the quieter side

North and west of Block 1, Block 5 and the neighbouring Lunugamvehera National Park see a fraction of the traffic. The landscape is different — more riverine forest, tall trees and rock pools along the Menik Ganga — and it forms a corridor that elephants use to move between parks.

Leopards are harder to find here, but the sightings are often more natural: an animal crossing the track ahead of you, resting on a branch above a river or walking unhurried along the road. You may see sloth bears, elephants, crocodiles and hornbills without another vehicle in sight.

### Who it suits

Photographers, returning visitors and anyone who prefers quality over a checklist. I often plan one drive in Block 1 and one in the quieter blocks, so you have the best of both.

## Reading the signs

A good tracker finds leopards with his ears as much as his eyes:

1. **Alarm calls** — the sharp bark of spotted deer, or langur monkeys shouting from the treetops.
2. **Pug marks** — fresh prints in the sand, read for direction and age.
3. **Behaviour of other animals** — peacocks staring in one direction, a herd of deer frozen in place.
4. **Time and temperature** — leopards move most in the first two hours of light and again in the late afternoon.

## Ethics on safari

I follow a simple standard on every drive: engine off at sightings, no off-road driving, no feeding, no blocking an animal's path, and voices low. It makes for better photographs and better memories — and it keeps Yala wild.

## When to go

February to June is generally the best season for leopards. Parts of Block 1 usually close for a few weeks from September to mid-October, when Block 5, Lunugamvehera and Bundala remain open.

If you would like to plan a leopard safari the quiet way, [share your dates with me](/contact) and I will match the blocks, the camp and the tracker to your trip.
